claims.claim: Maureen Eichner notes that A Wizard of Earthsea begins with the land, situating the reader physically and geographically.
claims.source: Maureen Eichner, 'Ursula Le Guin Reading Notes: A Wizard of Earthsea', By Singing Light
claims.quote: The story actually begins with the land
claims.page: paragraph on tone and prose style

claims.claim: Maureen Eichner reads Ged as treated with detachment and clear-sightedness by the narration.
claims.source: Maureen Eichner, 'Ursula Le Guin Reading Notes: A Wizard of Earthsea', By Singing Light
claims.quote: he is also treated with detachment and clear-sightedness
claims.page: paragraph on tone and prose style

claims.claim: Maureen Eichner characterises the book's register as a heightened and at the same time tightened prose style.
claims.source: Maureen Eichner, 'Ursula Le Guin Reading Notes: A Wizard of Earthsea', By Singing Light
claims.quote: a heightened and at the same time tightened prose style
claims.page: paragraph on tone and prose style

claims.claim: Maureen Eichner distinguishes Le Guin from Tolkien by the sense that not a single word is used unnecessarily.
claims.source: Maureen Eichner, 'Ursula Le Guin Reading Notes: A Wizard of Earthsea', By Singing Light
claims.quote: not a single word being used unnecessarily
claims.page: paragraph on tone and prose style

claims.claim: Copy-editor Stan Carey defines the plain style by clear syntax, precise word choice, natural emphasis and unobtrusive grammar.
claims.source: Stan Carey (copy-editor), ''How to see one's own world': Ursula K. Le Guin on writing style', Sentence first
claims.quote: clear syntax, precise word choice, natural emphasis, and unobtrusive grammar
claims.page: the author's own inserted paragraph on plain language

claims.feature: other: reference works a writer uses
claims.claim: Le Guin's 1989 note, quoted by Carey, names Strunk and White corrected by Miller and Swift as her road-atlas to English.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 1989 note to 'Dreams Must Explain Themselves', quoted by Stan Carey, Sentence first
claims.quote: are my road-atlas to English, and have never led me astray
claims.page: quotation from the 1989 revised Women's Press edition

claims.claim: The 1989 revised Women's Press text quoted by Carey reads 'the careless reader's even noticing' where the 1973 Pendragon text reads 'the careless readers even noticing'.
claims.source: Stan Carey quoting the 1989 revised edition of 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie', Sentence first
claims.quote: without the careless reader's even noticing

claims.claim: Le Guin states that prose often has three or even four unstressed syllables between stressed ones, where poetry seldom has more than two.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: Prose often has three or even four unstressed syllables

claims.claim: Le Guin says the absence of noticeable metrical regularity is the only difference between prose and poetry she has ever been certain of.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: the only difference between prose and poetry that I have

claims.claim: Le Guin proposes that stress-rhythm in prose has two elements, actual syllabic stresses and syntactical word groups she calls bars.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: two elements to stress-rhythm in prose: first, actual syllabic stresses

claims.claim: Le Guin says the bars of prose follow syntax, punctuation, sense, stress and breath.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: following syntax, punctuation, sense, stress, and breath

claims.claim: Le Guin asserts that good prose does have a stress-rhythm, however subtle and changing.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: good prose does have a stress-rhythm, subtle

claims.claim: Le Guin says dull prose, clunky narrative and hard-to-read textbook writing lack the rhythm that moves the reader.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: Dull prose, clunky narrative, hard-to-read textbook stuff, lacks the rhythm

claims.claim: Le Guin reports that her own prose samples run higher than the twenty-to-forty stresses per hundred syllables Judson Jerome gives for prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: My samples of prose run higher than that.
claims.page: after the eight scanned hundred-syllable samples

claims.claim: In Le Guin's hundred-syllable scansion the Tolkien sample carries 47 stresses, behind 'The Three Bears' and Woolf at 48.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.page: comparison table, 'Number of stresses, most to fewest'
